beats.narration: Chapter 23 is the densest chapter I have worked on so far. It spans seven sections covering the introduction to chemotherapy, principles of treatment, classes of chemotherapeutic agents, pharmacology, drug resistance, side effects, and a summary. The chapter carries 474 sentences, and 136 of them were flagged for verification. Almost every paragraph contains a drug name, a trial result, a dosing formula, or a regulatory fact.

beats.new_visual_element: The venetoclax finding, what the textbook says against the label
beats.narration: The most critical finding involves patient safety. The textbook presents venetoclax for multiple myeloma as established practice, but this use is not FDA-approved. The FDA label actually carries a mortality warning against that exact combination. The CANOVA phase III trial, published in January 2026, missed its primary endpoint and showed more treatment-emergent deaths in the venetoclax arm. This is the kind of error that could directly affect patient care.

beats.new_visual_element: What the textbook says, and what the record says
beats.narration: I also found errors reaching back into the history of chemotherapy. The textbook dates arsenicals to the 1900s, but Heinrich Lissauer treated leukemia with arsenic in 1865, thirty-five years earlier. It attributes nitrogen mustard research to World War One, when it came from World War Two. And the methotrexate half-life is stated backwards relative to the FDA label, which matters because rescue timing depends on it.

beats.new_visual_element: Three audits, and what each one caught
beats.narration: What made this chapter different is the quality control. I ran three full audits: the science, then every source re-fetched and confirmed on the page, then my deliverables against the instructions. They caught five errors in my own work, including two quotations attributed to the wrong papers and one verdict I reversed myself, on dexrazoxane, after reading the 2025 evidence.

beats.narration: Chapter 23 taught me something important: auditing AI-generated text is not enough. You also have to audit yourself. The same failure the textbook has, citing sources that do not say what you claim, can happen to the reviewer. That is why I built in multiple passes. One practical flag: files two through five carry a character encoding defect that corrupts Greek letters, and it has to be fixed before any text edits, or find and replace will silently fail.
